input:
Situation: A teammate posts that the project’s target audience is university students. An earlier decision with the same target and scope says the audience is college students; the new author says they are relaying the team’s agreed wording, not proposing a revision.
Request: Determine whether the new statement repeats the existing decision or conflicts with it.
How should I respond?

Situation: A new member approves a different project title from the current title, but the message does not say whether the two titles refer to the same deliverable or to a separate presentation tagline.
Request: Compare the targets and mark the case for human confirmation if the available context cannot establish whether the titles conflict.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team has approved youth housing as its project topic. A member jokes in chat, “Maybe we should throw away the topic and build a moon hotel instead, haha,” without any sign of an actual decision.
Request: Determine whether the joke should be compared with the approved topic or trigger an alert.
How should I respond?

Situation: The project’s approved target group is first-year students at the downtown campus. A new decision concerns first-year students at the west campus. Both entries use the topic_key “Target audience.”
Request: Compare the full targets and do not report a conflict if the campus scopes make the decisions distinct.
How should I respond?

Situation: The current approved decision says the project will cover rental affordability in two districts. A new approved decision says it will cover rental affordability in all districts, with no clear indication whether the original two-district scope is included or replaced.
Request: Compare the scopes and mark the pair as requiring confirmation if it is unclear whether the decisions can coexist.
How should I respond?

Situation: A member says, “Would a youth-housing topic work?” and another member’s message in the same comparison batch says, “We have finalized youth housing as the topic.”
Request: Exclude the question from decision comparison and treat the pair as unrelated rather than raising an alert.
How should I respond?

Situation: A student project team named Northstar is researching affordable housing for young adults. An approved team message says, “We’ll focus the report on rental deposits.” No earlier decision on the project scope exists.
Request: Classify the message and determine whether it is a decision that should be recorded for comparison.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate says, “We all agreed in the meeting to replace the project title ‘Housing First’ with ‘Rent Matters.’” The earlier title decision was made by one member.
Request: Compare the new decision with the earlier one and account for the reported team consensus.
How should I respond?

Situation: A message states, “The project will target students living off campus,” but the record does not identify who approved it, whether the team agreed, or whether it is only a suggestion.
Request: Assess whether the statement is sufficiently established as a decision; if its approval status is ambiguous, use confidence below 0.6 and hand it to a person.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate posts, “The student-housing report should cover rent, transport, and food,” while the group’s earlier confirmed scope covers rent and transport only. The new sentence does not indicate whether it is an agreed expansion or an idea.
Request: Determine whether the new scope is an approved change or a proposal, and avoid a confident conflict judgment without evidence of approval.
How should I respond?

Situation: The current decision says the project studies rental costs in one city. A new approved decision says the project studies transportation access in that same city. Both are under the broad topic_key “project scope.”
Request: Check whether the targets differ enough for both decisions to stand.
How should I respond?

Situation: An earlier decision says only first-year students will be surveyed. A different member, without team agreement, approves surveying all undergraduates. The broader scope includes the previously selected group but would change the survey’s target population.
Request: Assess the overlap and incompatibility of the scopes and determine whether to raise a conflict.
How should I respond?

Situation: An earlier decision says the team will survey only first-year students. A new decision says it will survey students from every year. The new record is from a different teammate and has no consensus evidence.
Request: Compare the overlapping populations and determine whether the broader scope removes or contradicts the existing restriction.
How should I respond?

Situation: The project team agreed to use an anonymous survey. A new message says, “Use the survey responses to identify each participant by name,” but does not explain whether this refers to a separate, consented dataset or the same anonymous survey.
Request: Compare the decisions, account for the unclear scope, and mark the case for human confirmation if necessary.
How should I respond?

Situation: A member records, “The team voted to switch from interviews to a survey,” and an earlier decision assigned interviews. The owner field identifies only the person who uploaded the record, not who approved the vote.
Request: Determine whether the explicit team agreement supports a change despite the uploader not being the decision-maker.
How should I respond?

Situation: A decision record says the team agreed in a meeting to use interviews instead of surveys, but the record does not name who approved it. An earlier individual decision by a different member specified surveys.
Request: Assess whether the meeting record establishes team consensus and select a judgment with an appropriate confidence score.
How should I respond?

Situation: An existing decision says the survey will target undergraduate students. A newly approved decision says the survey will target first-year undergraduates. The original decision does not exclude any undergraduate year.
Request: Assess whether the narrower statement preserves the original scope or replaces it.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team has an approved detailed-topic list containing “Survey audience.” A new decision says the survey will target first-year students, while an older decision filed under “Research plan” says it will target all undergraduates. The targets appear to be the same survey audience.
Request: Compare the same target even though the topic keys differ, prioritizing same-topic records where applicable, and provide a judgment.
How should I respond?

Situation: A member says, “Everyone agreed in yesterday’s meeting to use the shorter questionnaire,” but the meeting record shows only that the option was discussed and does not list attendees or a vote.
Request: Evaluate whether the statement establishes team consensus or whether the approval status needs human verification.
How should I respond?

Situation: A member posts, “The policy requires 90-day retention,” followed by, “We should keep the data for 90 days.” The team’s existing decision is to delete raw responses after 30 days, and the second sentence is a recommendation rather than an accepted outcome.
Request: Separate the reported external condition from the unapproved recommendation and avoid treating the recommendation as a final team decision.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team member approves a decision saying “Use 20 participants for the pilot,” but the earlier decision merely says “Use a small pilot group” and does not define a number. The member and team agreement status are unclear.
Request: Determine whether the new number is a compatible elaboration or an incompatible change, and lower confidence if the context is insufficient.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team has already approved a decision to use interviews as its research method. A new message says, “We found that interviews provide richer explanations,” but does not say the team has changed its method.
Request: Classify the new message as research information unless it clearly records an approved outcome, and avoid treating it as a new decision.
How should I respond?

Situation: The current decision records that the team selected a nonprofit as its case study. A new message says, “The nonprofit’s director prefers that we use a different organization,” but the team has not adopted that preference.
Request: Distinguish reported external information from an approved team decision and determine whether comparison is appropriate.
How should I respond?

Situation: A message says, “We decided to use the new survey platform, but we have not chosen which platform yet.” It expresses a team outcome at a broad level while leaving the specific target value unresolved.
Request: Determine which part, if any, is a confirmed decision and avoid inventing a final value for the unchosen platform.
How should I respond?

Situation: The current decision is “Use interviews for the tenant study,” recorded under “Research method.” A new approved decision says, “Use a survey for the tenant study,” but its topic key is “Data collection.” Both concern the method for the same study.
Request: Compare the decisions by their targets rather than treating different topic keys as proof that they are unrelated.
How should I respond?

Situation: A sentence says, “Let’s use a case-study approach, and I’ll draft the methods section by Friday.” The first clause is an agreed research decision; the second assigns a task.
Request: Split the sentence and classify each part independently, sending only the decision to comparison.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate posts, “We chose the title ‘Affordable Rooms’; I’ll finish the survey summary by Friday.” The title is already a confirmed project decision, while the survey summary is a new assigned task.
Request: Split the sentence into separate content parts, classify each part independently, and compare only the decision part with existing decisions.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team’s agreement says, “Collect responses only from current university students.” A member records, “Include recent graduates as well,” without noting team approval; it is unclear whether “as well” expands the target population or replaces the original restriction.
Request: Assess whether the scopes can coexist and use a confidence below 0.6 with a confirmation handoff if the wording remains ambiguous.
How should I respond?

Situation: Two team members disagree about whether a discussion in a meeting constituted consensus. One says the team approved online interviews; another says the matter was left open. The new decision’s owner and approval status are unclear.
Request: Avoid making a confident change-or-conflict judgment and leave the case for human confirmation if confidence is below 0.6.
How should I respond?

Situation: A student project team has an existing approved decision that its report will use regression analysis. The same student who made that decision now says the team has agreed to use cluster analysis instead.
Request: Classify the new statement and compare it with the current decision. Return the judgment, a one-line reason, and confidence.
How should I respond?

Situation: An earlier decision to use regression analysis was superseded by a team agreement to use cluster analysis. A new member now proposes correlation analysis as the final method.
Request: Compare the new approved decision with the current decision, not the superseded one, and report the judgment.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team has confirmed that its project will focus on housing affordability. A member says, “The article suggests housing affordability is getting worse,” without agreeing to change the project focus.
Request: Classify the statement as research information or a decision, and determine whether it should enter decision comparison.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate records, “I heard the team agreed to use cluster analysis,” but the meeting notes show no such agreement and the recorded owner is unclear.
Request: Compare the decision cautiously, and leave it for human confirmation with confidence below 0.6 if agreement or ownership cannot be established.
How should I respond?

Situation: A new record says the “survey analysis” will use regression, while an existing decision says the “report’s main analysis” will use cluster analysis. The project records do not explain whether these refer to the same analysis target.
Request: Compare the targets rather than assuming they are identical based on the shared analysis terminology; request confirmation if their relationship is ambiguous.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate says, “We agreed not to share raw survey responses outside the team.” The decision concerns privacy practices for the student-housing project, but an earlier record uses the topic_key “data handling.”
Request: Classify this as a relevant team decision and compare it with any earlier decision about the same data-sharing target.
How should I respond?

Situation: A member quotes an earlier message saying, “We should use interviews,” and then writes, “That was only a suggestion; we have now agreed on a survey.” The quote is not a current decision, while the survey is confirmed.
Request: Distinguish quoted proposal text from the newly approved decision before comparison.
How should I respond?

Situation: A new decision says, “Use the shorter questionnaire for the pilot,” while the current decision says, “Use the full questionnaire for the final study.” Both concern questionnaires, but they apply to distinct stages.
Request: Compare the scope and determine whether both decisions can remain valid.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team’s existing decision is “Use a survey for the student research.” A different member approves “Use interviews for the cafeteria-manager research.” Both are research-method decisions, but their target populations differ.
Request: Compare the targets before the subtopic and determine whether these decisions can coexist.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate writes, “I prefer Provider A because its dashboard is easier to use.” The project is comparing data tools, but the message describes only the writer’s personal preference and does not record team approval.
Request: Distinguish an individual preference from a confirmed team decision and avoid comparing it as one.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate posts, “We agreed in today’s meeting to set the app’s initial waste estimate using the campus survey results.” No earlier decision on the estimate is recorded.
Request: Recognize the stated team consensus as an approved decision and compare it with valid existing decisions.
How should I respond?

Situation: The Northstar team’s current decision is to use a 5-question user survey. A teammate approves a 10-question survey, but the record does not say whether it is the same survey, a separate follow-up, or a replacement.
Request: Check whether the targets and scopes are sufficiently clear to compare; use low confidence and request confirmation if they are not.
How should I respond?

Situation: An approved decision is recorded as “Use the newer dataset,” but the source message does not identify the dataset, the owner is unknown, and two valid datasets could fit the description. The closest existing decision concerns a different dataset.
Request: Avoid an unsupported comparison, assign confidence below 0.6, and leave the case for a person to resolve.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team agreed to support Claude only if there is enough time. A new member posts that the product will support ChatGPT only, without clarifying whether Claude support is still possible under the condition.
Request: Compare the decisions and, if their compatibility is unclear, mark the result as requiring human confirmation.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team has an approved decision to support ChatGPT only. An earlier conditional decision said that Claude could also be supported if time remained. The records do not clarify whether the team still expects to add Claude if time allows.
Request: Compare the decisions and, if their conditions make coexistence unclear, mark the result as requiring human confirmation with confidence below 0.6.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate writes, “Provider A seems cheapest; should we switch to it?” The current approved choice is Provider B, and the new message is a question without an agreed outcome.
Request: Keep the proposal or question out of decision comparison and avoid raising a conflict alert.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team approved including a browser extension in the MVP. A new decision says, “Include a browser extension that supports Chrome and Firefox,” and the new details do not remove the previously approved scope.
Request: Assess whether the new decision is a compatible elaboration or a change or conflict.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team decision says the prototype will support English. Another member’s approved decision says it will support English and Korean; the original decision does not say English is the only supported language.
Request: Determine whether adding Korean preserves the existing decision or changes its final value.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate approves the color of the project logo as navy. An earlier decision says the team’s uniform shirts will be navy. Both items are labeled with the detailed topic “branding,” but they concern separate objects.
Request: Compare the specific targets rather than treating the shared topic_key as evidence of conflict.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team decided that its final report would use a blue-and-white visual theme. Separately, it decided to use a blue background for the project website. Both records have the topic key “Design.”
Request: Decide whether these are conflicting decisions or distinct decisions that can both stand.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team decided to use the name Northstar for its project. A later decision sets the Northstar logo color to navy; both decisions have the same topic_key, “branding.”
Request: Compare the actual targets rather than relying on the shared topic_key, and determine whether both decisions can stand.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team decision states that the MVP excludes browser extensions. A new approved decision from another member says the extension is excluded from the first release but will be included in the later public launch. The team’s existing topic list uses “MVP scope.”
Request: Compare the decisions by their actual targets and scopes, rather than relying only on the matching topic label.
How should I respond?

Situation: The current decision is “Support ChatGPT only.” A newly approved decision says, “If we finish early, we can also support Claude.” The record does not say whether the first decision was intended to be permanent or conditional.
Request: Compare the pair and flag it for human confirmation if it is unclear whether both decisions can hold.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team member records a budget of $500. Another member records $650 for the same materials, but says only, “I think we should raise it,” and there is no evidence of approval.
Request: Distinguish a proposal from an approved decision and avoid comparing it as a final value.
How should I respond?

Situation: A decision says, “If the sponsor approves the design, use the compact layout.” Another member records, “Use the wide layout,” without saying whether sponsor approval occurred or whether the condition was met.
Request: Avoid assuming whether the conditional decision is active; assign confidence below 0.6 and mark the pair as requiring confirmation if necessary.
How should I respond?

Situation: A member writes, “Provider A costs $0.02 per request,” and the team’s current decision is to use Provider B. No one has approved a provider change.
Request: Classify the price statement as information and do not treat it as a new decision that conflicts with the current provider choice.
How should I respond?

Situation: A member writes, “Let’s keep the English-only version for the demo, then add Korean for the release.” The current decision says the demo will support English only, and the release decision has not yet been recorded.
Request: Separate the demo and release targets, and avoid treating compatible decisions for different stages as a conflict.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate writes, “Keep the first version unchanged for the pilot,” while the existing decision says to revise the interface before the public launch. The pilot and public launch are separate stages.
Request: Compare the scopes and determine whether the different stage-specific decisions are compatible.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team has already approved a poster size of A1. A new message says, “The print shop recommends A0,” without any indication that the team accepted the recommendation.
Request: Classify the statement as outside advice or research rather than a new approved poster-size decision.
How should I respond?

Situation: A hackathon team building a campus-navigation app has an approved decision from Mina to exclude offline maps from the MVP. Joon, without mentioning a team discussion, approves adding offline maps to the MVP.
Request: Determine whether the new decision is the same, a change, a conflict, or unrelated to the existing decision, and provide confidence.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team member recorded “browser extension excluded from MVP” under “MVP scope.” Another member later records “browser extension included” under “feature list,” with no evidence of agreement.
Request: Compare the decisions even though their topic_key values differ, and classify the incompatible outcomes.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team member writes, “I compared three API providers and Provider A is cheapest, so we have decided to use Provider A.” No earlier provider decision is recorded.
Request: Separate the research finding from the approved outcome, classify both parts, and identify which part should be sent for decision comparison.
How should I respond?

Situation: Two decision records disagree about the color of the same landing-page button: one says green and one says orange. Both are attributed to “Alex,” but the account may be shared by two teammates.
Request: Compare the values while accounting for uncertainty about whether the decisions came from the same person; request human confirmation if needed.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team member posts, “I prefer Claude to ChatGPT.” The project uses AI tools, but the member does not say the team selected Claude or changed an existing choice.
Request: Determine that a personal preference is not an approved team decision and do not compare it as one.
How should I respond?

Situation: A decision says the report will include three case studies. A later decision says it will include a case study from Seoul; the wording does not say whether this is one of the three or an additional case.
Request: Compare the scope and use confidence below 0.6 with a confirmation request if the new detail could either preserve or expand the existing decision.
How should I respond?

Situation: A member records, “The team agreed to remove the budget section,” but the only earlier record says the section was “not yet decided.”
Request: Check whether there is an existing valid decision to change, and avoid labeling the new outcome a conflict with an unapproved proposal or undecided item.
How should I respond?

Situation: A member says, “The draft currently uses a blue background.” This describes the document’s present state, but gives no indication that the team has approved blue as the final design.
Request: Distinguish a description of the current artifact from a confirmed decision and exclude it from comparison if it is not an agreed outcome.
How should I respond?

Situation: A message says, “Change the prototype to dark mode,” but it is unclear whether the speaker is issuing an approved team decision, making a request to a designer, or suggesting an option.
Request: Assess whether the message expresses a confirmed outcome; if approval status is ambiguous, keep confidence below 0.6 and ask a person to decide.
How should I respond?

Situation: The current database decision is “Use MySQL.” A teammate requests, “Please design the tables assuming MySQL,” without stating a new decision or change.
Request: Assess whether the request presupposes the existing decision and whether an alert is warranted.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team has agreed to use MySQL. A teammate asks an AI, “Please design the tables based on MySQL,” treating that choice as settled rather than announcing a new choice.
Request: Classify the request and determine how it should compare with the existing database decision.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team context supplied to the agent contains a team name and project topic but omits the enabled subtopic list and existing detailed-topic list. A new approved decision arrives about the report’s target audience.
Request: Classify and compare the decision as far as possible, and identify whether missing context requires a low-confidence human handoff.
How should I respond?

Situation: The current decision is “Use a blue cover.” A new decision says, “Use a blue cover with a white title,” and does not remove or contradict the existing color choice.
Request: Determine whether the added detail preserves the existing scope and classify the pair.
How should I respond?

Situation: A new decision says, “The final report will use APA style.” An earlier record says, “Use APA citations in the literature review.” It is unclear whether the earlier choice applied only to that section or to the entire report.
Request: Compare the scope carefully and request human confirmation with low confidence if the decisions’ scopes cannot be resolved.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team has agreed to support Claude if there is enough time. A different member now records that the product will support ChatGPT only, but it is unclear whether “only” excludes Claude even if time permits.
Request: Compare the decisions and, if their compatibility is unclear, mark the result as requiring human confirmation with confidence below 0.6.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team has chosen “North Star” as its team name. A later approved decision says the North Star logo will be navy blue; the matching words refer to different targets.
Request: Compare the team-name decision and logo-color decision, and determine whether both can stand.
How should I respond?

Situation: The detailed-topic list contains “App launch” and “App icon.” The team has decided the app will launch after the event, and a new member approves making the icon round; the new record mistakenly uses the “App launch” topic key.
Request: Compare the actual targets before using the topic key and determine the judgment.
How should I respond?

Situation: The Northstar team has an approved decision that the app’s name is “Northstar.” Under the same topic key, “Brand details,” another member approves making the logo a four-point star.
Request: Determine whether the two decisions conflict or can coexist, even though they share a topic key and a word.
How should I respond?

Situation: The current approved decision is to use a 12-question survey. A teammate records, “The survey should have 12 questions, including two questions about rent,” without adding to or replacing the existing questions.
Request: Determine whether this is a compatible elaboration of the existing decision or a change.
How should I respond?

Situation: A recorded team decision says to present the survey results as percentages. A new approved decision says to show the results as both percentages and counts, explicitly retaining percentages.
Request: Determine whether the elaboration preserves the existing scope or changes the final value.
How should I respond?

Situation: A valid earlier decision says, “If the team has extra time, add a chatbot.” A new decision says, “Support only the rent calculator.” The records do not clarify whether the chatbot would be excluded if time remains.
Request: Compare the conditional and unconditional scopes, and mark the pair as requiring human confirmation with confidence below 0.6 if coexistence is unclear.
How should I respond?

Situation: The existing decision is to add a chatbot only if there is extra time. The new decision says the MVP will include a chatbot, and the team has confirmed that the project has extra time.
Request: Assess whether the condition is now satisfied and whether the new decision changes or agrees with the existing one.
How should I respond?

Situation: The recorded decision says the team will not include a login feature. A new decision stored under a different subtopic name says login will be included. Both statements refer to the same feature and release scope.
Request: Compare the actual targets even though the topic keys differ.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team agreed to submit a ten-page report. A later decision says that the ten-page report will include a three-page methods section, leaving the original page limit unchanged.
Request: Decide whether the added detail changes or conflicts with the existing decision.
How should I respond?

Situation: The record contains two decisions about the same deliverable: one by Alex and one by Jamie. A new message says “we decided to shorten it,” but does not say who agreed or identify the meeting or participants.
Request: Assess whether the new decision can be compared confidently or requires human confirmation.
How should I respond?

Situation: A team member writes, “We decided the report will not include survey results,” but earlier in the same message says the team has already approved including those results. The intended final value is unclear.
Request: Compare the statements only if possible, and leave the ambiguous pair for human confirmation.
How should I respond?

Situation: A message says, “The draft might be 20 pages if we include all the interviews.” It describes a possible outcome, not an approved report length, while the current decision limits the report to 12 pages.
Request: Determine whether the hypothetical estimate is a decision that should be compared.
How should I respond?

Situation: The project has a confirmed decision to use blue for the charts. A new message says the cover page will be blue. The same color appears in both decisions, but the objects are different.
Request: Judge whether the decisions are unrelated despite sharing a value and a broad design topic.
How should I respond?

Situation: The Northstar team agreed to support ChatGPT first. An approved decision says, “If we finish early, we may also support Claude.” Another member now approves “ChatGPT only.” The records do not clarify whether the conditional option was adopted or remains possible.
Request: Compare the decisions, and if it is unclear whether their conditions can coexist, leave the case for human confirmation with confidence below 0.6.
How should I respond?

Situation: The current decision says to support ChatGPT only. An earlier conditional decision said to add Claude if time permits; the team has not recorded whether that condition has been met.
Request: Compare the conditional and unconditional decisions, using low confidence and requesting confirmation if coexistence cannot be established.
How should I respond?

Situation: The Northstar team has no existing detailed topic for a newly approved decision that the prototype will use a weekly leaderboard. The existing detailed-topic list includes “Rewards” and “Dashboard,” but neither clearly names the leaderboard.
Request: Classify the decision and identify an appropriate new detailed topic rather than forcing it into an unrelated existing topic.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate approves “The prototype will display a weekly leaderboard.” An existing decision says the dashboard will use green buttons. Both decisions are in the “Dashboard” topic, but concern different interface targets.
Request: Compare the actual targets and avoid treating the shared topic key as proof of a conflict.
How should I respond?

Situation: Two approved decisions concern the same report: one says “about 10 pages,” and another says “exactly 8 pages.” The owners are different, and the records do not clarify whether “about 10” permits 8 pages.
Request: Treat the pair as ambiguous, assign confidence below 0.6, and leave the judgment for human confirmation.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team chose the tagline “A home within reach.” Later, a member chooses the report’s section heading “Finding a home,” which has been stored under the same detailed topic_key, “project wording.”
Request: Compare the targets before treating the shared topic_key as evidence of a conflict.
How should I respond?

Situation: An approved decision says, “Do not include names in the public report.” A later member says, “Include participant names in the appendix,” without specifying whether the appendix will be public or private.
Request: Determine whether the two scopes overlap; if it is unclear whether the appendix is public, mark the pair as requiring confirmation.
How should I respond?

Situation: A new project decision concerns a feature area absent from the team’s existing detailed-topic list. The content is clearly related and approved, but it may establish a new grouping.
Request: Classify the decision, identify it as a new detailed topic when appropriate, and still compare it with earlier valid decisions about the same target.
How should I respond?

Situation: A project member writes, “The client approved the blue layout, so we will use it for the final prototype.” The team’s current design decision is green, and the client’s approval is recorded as authoritative for the project.
Request: Separate the external approval from the team’s adopted outcome as needed, then compare the confirmed final layout decision with the current one.
How should I respond?

Situation: An earlier decision assigns the live presentation to Yuna. A new decision assigns Seojun to create the presentation slides; both decisions are recorded under a broad presentation-related topic.
Request: Check whether the two decisions can coexist and classify their relationship.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team agreed that Yuna will give the presentation. A later decision assigns Seojun to prepare the slide deck; both responsibilities can be fulfilled.
Request: Compare the decisions and explain whether they are unrelated despite both being associated with the presentation.
How should I respond?

Situation: An earlier decision assigns Yuna to deliver the presentation. A new decision assigns Seojun to create the presentation slides. Both records are categorized under presentation work.
Request: Check whether the targets are actually the same before treating the different owners as a conflict.
How should I respond?

Situation: A message says, “The service name is SyncUp, and I’ll finish the research summary by Thursday.” The first clause was approved in the team chat; the second is the speaker volunteering for a task. The sentence also includes the speaker’s private phone number in the task text.
Request: Split and classify the two clauses separately, mask the phone number, and compare only any approved decision.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team has a recorded decision to meet at 3 p.m. A message says, “Let’s meet at 4 p.m. next week instead,” but it is unclear whether the sender has authority to change the schedule or is merely making a suggestion.
Request: Assess the ambiguity about approval and choose a confidence level that sends the case for confirmation if it is below 0.6.
How should I respond?

Situation: The team’s decisions list “Mobile app = after the event” and “App icon = rounded square.” The new decision says “The app must be ready before the event,” and the topic labels are inconsistent.
Request: Compare the decision with the relevant existing target and distinguish it from similarly named but separate targets.
How should I respond?

Situation: A decision record lists two owners because the meeting notes name both the speaker and the person who proposed the outcome. A new conflicting decision comes from one of those people, but the record does not show who actually approved the earlier decision.
Request: Do not infer decision authority from ambiguous owner metadata; assign low confidence and hand the comparison to a person.
How should I respond?

Situation: A current decision sets the report deadline for Friday. The same owner later records, “Change our internal draft deadline to Thursday,” while the professor’s final submission deadline remains Friday.
Request: Compare the internal draft target separately from the external submission deadline and determine whether the decisions can coexist.
How should I respond?

Situation: A teammate says, “The professor’s announcement says the final report is due May 20.” The team has already decided internally to finish its draft by May 16.
Request: Distinguish the external submission condition from the internal work deadline and determine whether they conflict.
How should I respond?

Situation: A member writes, “The customer interview summary is ready, and I’ll upload it by Friday.” The team has an existing detailed topic called “Interview summary,” but no decision about who will upload it.
Request: Classify the content as a team task rather than a decision, and extract the responsible person and due date if the available context allows.
How should I respond?

Situation: A member posts, “I’ll prepare the literature review by Thursday.” The project is a team report, but no earlier decision about that task’s content exists.
